body.text: Several recent incidents have revealed the depth and breadth of the false case discourse. The death by suicide of the Bangalore-based engineer Atul Subhash led to an outcry against laws on dowry, domestic violence, and cruelty; Subhash’s death was seen as the outcome of harassment by his wife and her family.

Accusations of harassment of the Telugu film industry choreographer Jani Master have also been labelled false, the result of a conspiracy or deliberate fabrication on the part of the complainant. Discussions of false cases pervade social life. False cases are a topic of conversation and concern within traditional and social media, in classrooms and courtrooms, and in personal discussions with friends and family. Such discussions usually revolve around women, painting them as filing complaints that they know to be untrue, either out of a vindictive desire to harass men, or because they seek leverage in an existing conflict.

The flipside of this is the idea of victimised men, who are vulnerable to a legal system that is biased against them, that will harass and penalise not just them but their families on the basis of a single complaint. The idea of false cases is paired with that of the misuse of law—that certain laws are not used for the purpose for which they were intended, but rather are invoked only to harass, threaten, or blackmail. The false case discourse also extends to certain other communities, most noticeably Scheduled Caste communities, with similar discourses and ideas surrounding the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.

And yet the discourse of false cases hides more than it reveals. With its focus on laws pertaining to violence against women, it fails to examine the nature and extent of misuse of other domains of civil and criminal law. It also fails to engage with the realities behind false cases. Who files cases where they know that the allegations made are untrue? Why and under what circumstances? What is the role of the police and investigative agencies in this regard? What happens when specific sets of cases are assumed to be false? How do these assumptions circulate and take hold, and what impact do they have?

These and similar questions drove the discussions at the National Conference on the Dynamics of False Cases, held at the Kautilya School of Public Policy, GITAM (deemed to be University), in August. The conference, jointly organised by the Kautilya School of Public Policy, Yugantar, the International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, and Bhumika Women’s Collective, explored the phenomenon of false cases through engagements with academics, journalists, activists, development sector professionals, and others.

What is meant by a false case? Advocate Disha Wadekar notes that there is no such thing as a “false case” in any criminal statute. The only mention of false cases in law is within the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, which has a section on false complaints. Even here, a separate enquiry needs to be conducted to determine if a case is false—the lack of evidence, complaints not being upheld, etc., do not establish falsity.
And yet the idea of false cases being a widespread phenomenon is ubiquitous. Where does this idea come from?

One common argument in favour of deeming large swathes of cases to be false is that these cases often end in acquittals. The low conviction rates in cases of rape, cruelty, caste atrocity, etc., are deemed to be evidence that large numbers of such cases are false.

Such an understanding overlooks the fact that acquittals may occur for a variety of reasons. Flavia Agnes, noted lawyer and women’s rights activist, observes that cases can be weakened by a variety of factors: for example, retractions by witnesses and victims, or witnesses turning hostile. There is little popular understanding of the many pressures on victims and the difficulties and lack of support they encounter as they attempt to pursue their cases through the judicial system. These often cause them to turn hostile or simply become unable to continue to pursue justice. Cases are then weakened, leading to acquittals, and these acquittals in turn feed the false case narrative.

Agnes also describes how, in cruelty cases, the victim’s statement is recorded by the police. These statements may be recorded haphazardly, with the police leaving out many details. Victims themselves are not able to insist on their statements being recorded accurately and thoroughly. Judges later review these allegations and hold the lack of detail and vagueness against the victims, reading them as inconsistencies that indicate fabrication.

Professor Mrinal Satish of the National Law School of India University, Bengaluru, also observes that the police have their own ideas of what justice and fair punishments look like. A sympathetic police officer may advise exaggeration or fabrication in order to strengthen a complaint. These fabricated narratives will not hold up to scrutiny as the case proceeds, and there may be an acquittal down the line. By then, however, the accused may have been in pre-trial detention for months, and functionaries in the criminal justice system may deem this punishment enough.

Delay in filing cases is also held against complainants. Agnes points out various reasons why women do not file cases of cruelty. One is the need to save their marriages. Women know that when they file a complaint of cruelty, their marriage will be over; this prevents them from filing cases immediately after the cruelty occurs. Sometimes, complaints may be filed years after the incident, often when the husbands file for divorce. Both Agnes and Hyderabad-based advocate Vasudha Nagaraj point out that such delayed complaints are then held against women. Nagaraj also states that over time, women’s recollections of specific parts of incidents might fade—for instance, what clothes they were wearing when the incident occurred, the specific time of day it took place, etc. This lack of detail, again, is held against them.

Many speakers observe that it is the police and lawyers who often advise women to file false cases. Kondaveeti Satyavati of the Bhumika Women’s Collective notes that at the time of divorce, women often only want maintenance and child custody; however, police and lawyers advise them to file all possible cases against all family members, persuading them that this will help their cause. They are also told to file cases of cruelty against husbands reluctant to pay maintenance and child support, as a way to bring them to the negotiating table.
How false cases enter public discourse

How do such cases circulate in the public? Journalist Dhanya Rajendran has described the patterns in media reports of cases of violence against women. When the cases first become public, the focus is the case itself: the people involved, the allegations, the response of the accused, and so on. Within a few days, the attention often shifts to the victim. Their portrayal in the media often depends on how much the woman fits the idea of an “ideal victim”: someone who is respectable, conservative in dress, behaviour, and so on. The victim’s social media posts are scoured, her past examined, and aspersions cast on her character.

Wadekar notes that the caste of the ideal victim also matters, often taking the form of a “virtuous savarna woman”. The Bangalore-based activist Madhu Bhushan says that the “false cases” discourse is a red herring, a new means of circulating old tropes and stereotypes about good and bad women, tropes that have been used to “control and confine women".

The widespread idea of false cases has several impacts. Satyavati recounts the police often telling her that all laws are being misused—laws against cruelty, domestic violence, and sexual harassment. This idea often comes up during training sessions on sexual harassment, where the first questions raised by the audience are usually on false cases. Myths of misuse are so ingrained that filing cases can become difficult; Agnes, for example, mentions the difficulty in filing cases of cruelty.

Engaging with the idea of false cases is, therefore, a difficult exercise. Although the term is ubiquitous, it contains within it a number of different issues, and different cases and allegations. Radhika Krishnan of IIITH and Tejaswini Madabhushi of Yugantar point out the insufficiency of language, with the term “false case” being applied both to cases where false allegations were knowingly made and to the large numbers of cases that are presumed to be false because of the social discourse surrounding them. Given this, should there be another term for cases presumed to be false due to the weight of the false-case myth?
The costs of the false-case myth

The myth also pits men and women against each other, with little examination of the systemic factors that impact them. Bhushan notes that men’s issues too need to be addressed, with male emotional vulnerability due to personal and structural stress a neglected area. Family problems, health issues, and livelihood fears are linked to male suicides, and need to be addressed outside a “men vs. women” framework.

Understanding the phenomena that get labelled “false cases”—and those that are false but not termed as such—therefore requires a new language, a new approach, and a deeper study of data. Most importantly, it requires a deeper engagement and disaggregation of phenomena, one that goes beyond simplistic, stereotyped understandings of “false” and “genuine”.
Vasudha Katju is an assistant professor at Kautilya School of Public Policy, Hyderabad.
